author: derekchiang
content:
i looked deeper into this -- as to whether we have to increase bandwidth requirements for 7870 for PQ-Gasper, the answer is definitely yes UNLESS we strongly optimize networking.  with today’s gossipsub setup we’d need to bump the 7870 requirements by A LOT

picture 1 is illustrative of the issue.  basically the voting window is when the bandwidth pressure is the strongest

i created this calculator for bandwidth requirements under different parameters: https://claude.ai/artifact/XVaC9kAcD8JagNXRr73Efy.  the default parameters assume today’s gossipsub setup, and you can see that the uplink traffic for attesters connected to 1 subnet goes up to 114 mbps (picture 2), way above 7870’s 25 mbps.  with the networking optimizations that <@439032863904628745> implemented in his simulator (e.g. reducing peer count + announcements), this drops to ~50 mbps, still much higher than 7870’s 25.  in my simulation, home nodes only fit into 7870 if we drop them off all subnets (like <@425567222635954178>'s simulation did) AND implement Kamil’s networking optimizations.  you can try changing the duplication factor or just click one of the presets under the “Network” section

author: nashatyrev
content:
<@421767904053297152> great tool 👍 
One small thing: the gossip duplication is effectively different for attestations (small messages) and aggregates (big messages). On my simulations they are around x9 and x6 respectfully. They also slightly differ across node types. 
```
1000 nodes, mesh ~9.6 peers/topic, one slot

Tier                    Votes    Aggregates
----------------------  -------  ----------
Pools                   9.1x     3.9x
VPS                     9.0x     3.4x
Upper home (200/100)    9.4x     4.2x
Mid home (100/50)       9.3x     6.3x
Home (50/25)            n/a *    5.6x
----------------------  -------  ----------
All nodes               9.1x     4.1x
```
* Effective avrg mesh size in simulations is around 10, but in a wild it could be around 8 due to peers rotation

author: .just_kk
content:
Forked Xray to show what CL gossip on a mainnet node would look like under PQ Gasper if we made no networking changes: https://college-locations-segments-pairs.trycloudflare.com (link is temporary).

A Prysm mainnet node sits behind a gateway that resizes messages:
- attestation signatures become XMSS-sized (2,404 B);
 - aggregates carry a 256 KB leanVM proof 

The node joins 8 attestation subnets instead of 2, because committees grow 4× (about 512 → 2048). The gateway keeps 1 in 16 aggregates, because aggregates drop from about 1024 per slot (64 committees × 16 aggregators) to about 64 (16 × 4). Sync-committee messages are dropped.

other messages are not changed / resized

author: tcoratger
content:
Hi everyone,

I don’t want to interrupt the current discussion, but I’d like to share a draft with you. Following the Cambridge workshop, it became clear that networking in the context of PQ requires some careful thought—going back to the discussions held before the Mumbai meeting (when topics like DC, FOCIL, etc., were still totally in the roadmap). Since Cambridge, I’ve been exploring a research approach that’s a bit unconventional for me, relying heavily on an agentic framework.

Here’s what I’ve done: I spent time organizing a vast amount of contextual information—conversations, research papers, blog posts, video transcripts, ACDs, EIPs, and so on—and compiled an overview of approaches taken by other projects, such as Celestia, Tempo, Solana, and Commonware. I then spent some time each day working iteratively with an AI agent to design a brand-new P2P protocol, custom-built for Ethereum within a PQ context.

Admittedly, this might seem quite far from the current discussion; since the Mumbai meeting, the focus has shifted toward the opposite approach—changing as little as possible to ensure PQ can be shipped as quickly as possible.

There are of course aspects that would need refinement to make the protocol viable and fully aligned with Ethereum’s constraints, but I’m quite pleased with the outcome—it contains a number of interesting ideas and concepts. Perhaps some of these could be adopted down the line or provide some inspiration for you as experts (as you’re likely aware, I’m not a P2P expert myself). In any case, I’d welcome your feedback. I believe the document is structured in a way that allows you to easily navigate it—perhaps using an AI agent—to extract the core ideas without needing to read the whole thing.
